steps.prompt: Both of these are about phones at lunch. Which one would convince a principal?
steps.a: Phones are good. My friend has a phone. You can call people. Some kids play games. Phones have cameras. Lunch is at twelve. I think we should have them.
steps.b: Should students be allowed to use phones at lunch? They should, because phones keep students in touch with family and teach them to manage their own time. … (three paragraphs of reasons and evidence) … Trusting students with phones at lunch is a small step toward trusting them to make good choices.
steps.reveal: B is shaped like an essay: it opens with a question (a hook) and a clear point (a thesis), gives its reasons one paragraph at a time, and ends by bringing the reader back to the point. A is a pile of thoughts in no order.

cards.title: An essay is a plan made visible
cards.body: An essay is a group of paragraphs that all work for one main point, the thesis. The classic shape has five paragraphs: an introduction, three body paragraphs and a conclusion.

cards.title: Each part has a job
cards.body: Introduction: grab the reader with a hook, then state the thesis. Body paragraphs: one reason or part each, with a topic sentence, evidence and explanation (just like Unit 10). Conclusion: restate the thesis in new words and leave a final thought.

cards.title: The five paragraphs at a glance
cards.text:
1. Introduction: Have you ever fallen asleep in first period? Schools should start later because teens need more sleep, focus better and are safer on the roads.
2. Body 1: Teens need more sleep than adults…
3. Body 2: Rested students focus better…
4. Body 3: Later starts make the roads safer…
5. Conclusion: A later start would give teens the sleep, focus and safety they need. Next time your school sets its timetable, ask for one more hour.
cards.note: Every body paragraph proves one part of the thesis: sleep, focus, safety.
